result:
The city hired a man to remove unnecessary signs.

His first assignment was a brass plaque on an ordinary brick wall:

**DO NOT THROW STONES AT THIS WALL.**

He stood in front of it for some time. There were no broken windows nearby. No loose stones. The wall itself seemed sturdy and unoffended.

He unscrewed the plaque.

Behind it, in faded blue paint, someone had written:

**PLEASE THROW STONES AT THIS WALL.**

This complicated matters.

He telephoned his supervisor, who told him to use his judgment. His judgment, after twenty-three years of municipal service, told him to have lunch.

When he returned, a little girl was studying the painted words.

“Are we supposed to?” she asked.

“No,” he said.

“Why does it say please?”

“Sometimes people are polite about the wrong things.”

She considered this, then went away.

The man painted over the words. While the paint dried, he sat on a bench across the street. Without its plaque, the wall looked larger. He noticed a climbing rose growing from the adjoining garden, its longest branch caught behind a drainpipe.

He freed the branch and laid it along the top of the wall. It sprang back. He tried again, securing it with a short length of string from his toolbox.

Then he gathered the screws, wrapped the plaque in his dust sheet, and filled in the job form.

Under **REASON FOR REMOVAL**, he wrote: *Unnecessary.*

Under **ADDITIONAL WORK COMPLETED**, he hesitated before writing: *Some gardening.*

By the following summer, the rose had covered the patch of fresh paint. People sometimes stopped to photograph it, usually standing well back so they could get the whole wall in.
